items.title: [joserfc] joserfc: Compact JWS size guard allocates attacker-controlled segments before rejection
items.summary: Summaryjoserfc 1.7.4 defines compact-JWS header, payload, and signature limits, butcalls value.split(b".") before validating them. Python bytes.split() copiesthe attacker-controlled segments, so the current guard allocates roughly onecomplete payload before rejecting it.Reproduction.venv-research/bin/python 06-practical-testing/preauth-memory-profile.pyThe input is resident before a fork-isolated verifier runs, and every signatureis invalid.InputPeak RSS deltaAmplificationResult1 MiB1.11 MiB1.11×size rejected4 MiB4.04 MiB1.01×size rejected8 MiB8.04 MiB1.01×size rejected16 MiB16.04 MiB1.00×size rejected32 MiB31.74 MiB0.99×size rejected64 MiB63.80 MiB1.00×size rejectedThe unconstrained profile is the primary evidence: joserfc allocates anadditional attacker-sized object before producing its intendedExceededSizeError. A separate baseline-plus-headroom stress test raisesMemoryError when that copy cannot fit, but this report does not characterizean absolute RLIMIT_AS value as a realistic worker memory budget.Security ArgumentThe issue is not that joserfc can prevent the transport layer from receiving alarge header. The issue is narrower: once bytes reach deserialize_compact(),the library's existing size guard cannot fulfill its allocation-limiting purposebecause attacker-controlled segment copies are created first.This differs fromGHSA-frfh-8v73-gjg4,which concerned embedding already-loaded oversized segments in exception and logmessages. Here, the current implementation itself creates an additionalpayload-sized allocation before its fixed size exception.Recommended FixCheck len(value) against a maximum compact-serialization size beforesplit(). If per-segment diagnostics are needed, locate delimiters with boundedfind() operations or memory views, validate offsets and lengths, and only thenmaterialize acceptable segments.Referenceshttps://github.com/authlib/joserfc/security/advisories/GHSA-9pg5-8c7x-5hfxhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119284https://github.com/authlib/joserfc/commit/397e04f4bbce0b94d86e31c1c003f4640af8fb39https://github.com/authlib/joserfc/releases/tag/1.7.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9pg5-8c7x-5hfx

items.title: [joserfc] joserfc: Unbounded JWE General JSON `recipients` Array Leads to CPU Exhaustion (DoS) via Repeated RSA Private-Key Decryption
items.summary: Summaryjoserfc.jwe.decrypt_json(), the library's public parser for JWE General JSON Serialization, accepts an attacker-controlled recipients array of unbounded length and performs one full private-key decryption operation (decrypt_cek) for every recipient present in the input, with no cap on recipient count. An unauthenticated network attacker who can send a JWE General JSON document to any endpoint that decrypts it with an RSA key (e.g. RSA-OAEP) can force the victim to perform an arbitrary, attacker-chosen number of RSA private-key decryption operations from a single, relatively small HTTP request. This gives the attacker a highly asymmetric CPU-exhaustion (Denial of Service) primitive: local reproduction shows request size growing linearly with recipient count (~396 bytes/recipient) while server-side CPU time grows in lock-step (near 1:1 ratio between recipient-count growth and decrypt-time growth), and the library's only documented mitigation knob, verify_all_recipients=False, does not reduce the CPU cost, since the decrypt loop attempts every recipient's decrypt_cek() unconditionally before that flag is ever consulted. This is CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption) with CVSS v3.1 Base Score 7.5 (High).Detailsjoserfc validates and caps several structural elements of a JWE (protected header size, encrypted key size, IV size, ciphertext size, and auth-tag size) inside src/joserfc/_rfc7516/registry.py, but performs no validation whatsoever on the number of entries in the recipients array of a JWE General JSON Serialization object.Data flow (source → sink), verified directly against the repository source at commit 26a10275e88276184f91ae2a6409647bfac7fea5 (joserfc 1.7.4):src/joserfc/jwe.py:214 — public parser entry point decrypt_json(data, private_key, ...). This is a documented, unauthenticated (at the library boundary) API for parsing externally supplied JWE JSON.src/joserfc/jwe.py:238 — if "recipients" is present in the input dict, extract_general_json(...) is invoked.src/joserfc/_rfc7516/json.py:84-86 — iterates for item in data["recipients"]: and appends a Recipient object for every entry, with no upper bound check on len(data["recipients"]):for item in data["recipients"]:    recipient = __extract_recipient(obj, item, registry)    obj.recipients.append(recipient)src/joserfc/jwe.py:252 — the private key is attached to every extracted recipient.src/joserfc/_rfc7516/message.py:103-112 — _perform_decrypt() loops over every recipient in obj.recipients and calls decrypt_recipient(...) for each one, regardless of how many there are:cek_set = set()for recipient in obj.recipients:    headers = recipient.headers()    registry.check_header(headers, True)    alg = registry.get_alg(headers["alg"])    try:        cek = decrypt_recipient(alg, enc, recipient, tag)        cek_set.add(cek)src/joserfc/_rfc7518/jwe_algs.py:74-83 — for RSA-OAEP/RSA1_5 recipients, this dispatches to the sink, a genuine RSA private-key operation:def decrypt_cek(self, recipient: Recipient[RSAKey]) -> bytes:    key = recipient.recipient_key    assert key is not None    self.check_key_type(key)    op_key = key.get_op_key("decrypt")    try:        assert recipient.encrypted_key is not None        cek = op_key.decrypt(recipient.encrypted_key, self.padding)Confirmed by direct inspection of src/joserfc/_rfc7516/registry.py: size caps exist for max_header_length, max_encrypted_key_length, max_iv_length, max_ciphertext_length, and max_auth_tag_length (registry.py:52-62, 103-121), but no max_recipients (or equivalent) field or check exists anywhere in registry.py, json.py, or jwe.py.Critically, the loop in message.py:103-112 calls decrypt_recipient() for every recipient unconditionally — this happens before registry.verify_all_recipients is ever consulted. Setting verify_all_recipients=False (the library's only documented related option) therefore changes whether a decrypt failure raises an exception, but does not reduce the number of RSA private-key operations performed, and thus does not mitigate the CPU cost. This was independently confirmed at runtime (see PoC results below): decrypt time is statistically identical between verify_all_recipients=True and verify_all_recipients=False for the same recipient count.decrypt_json() is not a demo-only or admin-only code path: it is documented in docs/guide/jwe.rst:156-182 as the standard way to parse and decrypt an externally received General JSON JWE, and requires no special/non-default configuration to trigger. This is functionally analogous to two other resource-exhaustion issues already fixed in the same codebase — the PBES2 p2c iteration cap (src/joserfc/_rfc7518/jwe_algs.py:237-239) and the JWE compression "zip bomb" size cap (src/joserfc/_rfc7518/jwe_zips.py:11,26-28) — indicating the recipient-count case was simply missed from the same class of hardening.PoCBoth static (Phase 1) and dynamic, containerized (Phase 2) reproduction confirmed the vulnerability against unmodified joserfc 1.7.4 source
